title: Review: Quadratic equations
description: Questions on the ideas in this guide, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: Why does the definition of a quadratic equation $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ require $$a \neq 0$$?
options: So that the quadratic formula never divides by zero, which is the only reason
Because with $$a = 0$$ the $$x^2$$ term disappears and the equation is linear
Because $$b$$ and $$c$$ must also be non-zero
Because otherwise the equation would have no solutions
questions.explanation: The condition $$a \neq 0$$ is what makes the equation quadratic (:ref{#quadratic}). With $$a = 0$$ it is $$bx + c = 0$$, a linear equation. The coefficients $$b$$ and $$c$$ may be $$0$$.

questions.question: Is $$x^2 - 5x = 0$$ a quadratic equation?
options: No, because it has no constant term
No, because it can be factored
Yes: only $$a$$ must be non-zero, and here $$a = 1$$, $$b = -5$$, $$c = 0$$
questions.explanation: A quadratic only needs $$a \neq 0$$ (:ref{#quadratic}). Either of the other coefficients may be $$0$$.

questions.question: What kind of equation is $$x^2 + 3x = x^2 + 6$$?
options: Linear: once in standard form the squares cancel, leaving $$3x = 6$$
questions.explanation: Whether an equation is quadratic is decided in standard form (:ref{#quadratic}). Subtracting $$x^2$$ from both sides is a safe step, and it leaves $$3x = 6$$, a linear equation with the single solution $$2$$.

questions.question: How many real solutions can a quadratic equation have?
options: Any number, depending on the coefficients
Two, one or none, and never more than two
questions.explanation: $$x^2 = 9$$ has two, $$x^2 = 0$$ has one and $$x^2 = -1$$ has none, and a quadratic never has more than two (:ref{#root-count}).

questions.question: What are the solutions of $$(x - 5)^2 = -3$$?
options: There are none, because a square is never negative
questions.explanation: By :ref{#shifted-square}, $$(x - s)^2 = k$$ has no solution when $$k < 0$$: no real number squares to a negative number (:ref{#real-numbers/squares-positive}).

questions.question: The proof that $$(x - s)^2 = k$$ has the solutions $$s \pm \sqrt{k}$$ when $$k > 0$$ rests on which earlier fact?
options: That $$y^2 = k$$ has exactly two solutions, $$\pm\sqrt{k}$$, so $$x - s$$ must be one of them
That a product is $$0$$ only when a factor is
That squaring both sides keeps every solution
questions.explanation: Writing $$y = x - s$$ turns the equation into $$y^2 = k$$, which is solved by :ref{#real-numbers/square-root-count}; then $$x = y + s$$ (:ref{#shifted-square}).

questions.question: Why does $$(x - 2)(x + 5) = 0$$ mean that $$x = 2$$ or $$x = -5$$?
options: Because the two brackets must be equal
Because a product is $$0$$ only when one of its factors is $$0$$
Because the sum of the brackets is $$0$$
questions.explanation: If a product is $$0$$, one of the factors is $$0$$ (:ref{#numbers/zero-product}), so $$x - 2 = 0$$ or $$x + 5 = 0$$ (:ref{#solve-by-factors}).

questions.question: A student solves $$(x - 1)(x - 2) = 6$$ by setting $$x - 1 = 6$$ or $$x - 2 = 6$$. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: it gives the right answers
They should set each bracket equal to $$3$$
They should divide both sides by $$x - 1$$
The zero product rule needs $$0$$ on one side; many pairs of numbers multiply to $$6$$
questions.explanation: Only $$0$$ forces a factor to be $$0$$ (:ref{#solve-by-factors}). Expand, move the $$6$$ across, and factor $$x^2 - 3x - 4 = (x + 1)(x - 4)$$ instead.

questions.question: Why is dividing both sides of $$x^2 = 5x$$ by $$x$$ a mistake?
options: It loses the solution $$x = 0$$: dividing is safe only by a number known not to be $$0$$
It gives a wrong value instead of $$5$$
It is fine, as long as you check the answer
questions.explanation: Dividing by a number is a safe step only when that number isn't $$0$$ (:ref{#linear-equations/safe-steps}), and whether $$x$$ is $$0$$ is what we don't know. Factoring $$x(x - 5) = 0$$ keeps both solutions, $$0$$ and $$5$$.

questions.question: To factor $$x^2 + bx + c$$ as $$(x + m)(x + n)$$, what must $$m$$ and $$n$$ satisfy?
questions.explanation: Multiplying out, $$(x + m)(x + n) = x^2 + (m + n)x + mn$$, so the sum must be $$b$$ and the product $$c$$ (:ref{#factoring-method}). Matching only the product is a common mistake.

questions.question: What are the solutions of $$(x + 3)(x - 4) = 0$$?
questions.explanation: Each factor is $$0$$ at the opposite of its number: $$x + 3 = 0$$ at $$x = -3$$ and $$x - 4 = 0$$ at $$x = 4$$ (:ref{#solve-by-factors}).

questions.question: Why can't $$x^2 + 49$$ be factored like $$x^2 - 49 = (x - 7)(x + 7)$$?
options: Because $$49$$ is not a perfect square
Because a factor $$x - k$$ would give a solution, and $$x^2 + 49 \ge 49$$ is never $$0$$
questions.explanation: If it split into real linear factors, the zero product rule would give a solution (:ref{#solve-by-factors}). But $$x^2 + 49$$ is always at least $$49$$, so it has no zeros; only a difference of squares factors this way (:ref{#numbers/square-formulas}).

questions.question: In the area picture of $$x^2 + 6x$$, what is missing to make a complete square of side $$x + 3$$?
options: Nothing: it is already a square
questions.explanation: The $$6x$$ is cut into two strips $$3$$ by $$x$$, which leave a corner of side $$\frac{6}{2} = 3$$ missing, so $$x^2 + 6x = (x + 3)^2 - 9$$ (:ref{#complete-square}).

questions.question: When completing the square on $$x^2 + bx = d$$, why must $$\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$$ be added to both sides?
options: Because adding the same number to both sides is a safe step, while adding to one side changes the equation
It only needs adding to the left side
questions.explanation: Adding the same number to both sides keeps exactly the same solutions (:ref{#linear-equations/safe-steps}). Adding it to one side alone gives a different equation (:ref{#complete-square}).

questions.question: How do you complete the square on $$2x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0$$?
options: Add $$\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^2$$ to both sides straight away
Divide the whole equation by $$2$$ first, so that $$x^2$$ stands on its own
questions.explanation: The method needs $$x^2$$ on its own. Dividing by a non-zero number is a safe step, and $$a \neq 0$$ in a quadratic (:ref{#quadratic}), so divide by $$2$$ and then complete the square (:ref{#complete-square}).

questions.question: Why does completing the square solve every quadratic, while factoring does not?
options: Because every quadratic has whole-number solutions
It doesn't: it fails when there is no solution
Because it turns any quadratic into a square equal to a number, which is always solvable or shown to have no solution
questions.explanation: Any $$x^2 + bx + c = 0$$ becomes $$\left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2}{4} - c$$ (:ref{#complete-square}), and :ref{#shifted-square} handles that in every case, including showing there is no solution.

questions.question: Where does the quadratic formula come from?
options: From completing the square on $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ once, with letters instead of numbers
It is assumed as a rule without proof
questions.explanation: The proof divides by $$a$$, completes the square, and takes square roots, all with letters (:ref{#quadratic-formula}).

questions.question: To solve $$3x^2 = 4x + 1$$ with the formula, what are $$a$$, $$b$$ and $$c$$?
options: $$a = 3$$, $$b = -4$$, $$c = -1$$, after moving everything to one side
questions.explanation: The formula needs the standard form $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ (:ref{#quadratic-formula}). Subtracting $$4x + 1$$ gives $$3x^2 - 4x - 1 = 0$$; the signs are part of the coefficients.

questions.question: In $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$, what is divided by $$2a$$?
questions.explanation: The whole top is divided by $$2a$$, which comes from halving $$\frac{b}{a}$$ when completing the square (:ref{#quadratic-formula}).

questions.question: What does the formula say about where the two solutions lie?
options: They sit the same distance either side of $$-\frac{b}{2a}$$
questions.explanation: The formula is $$-\frac{b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$: a centre plus or minus a distance (:ref{#quadratic-formula}). That centre is also where the parabola's vertex is (:ref{#vertex}).

questions.question: What does a discriminant $$b^2 - 4ac = 0$$ tell you?
options: The equation has exactly one solution, $$-\frac{b}{2a}$$
The equation has two solutions, one of them $$0$$
questions.explanation: Zero means exactly one solution (:ref{#root-count}). Only a negative discriminant means none.

questions.question: Why does only the sign of $$b^2 - 4ac$$ decide how many solutions there are?
options: Because completing the square gives $$\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}$$, and $$4a^2$$ is always positive
questions.explanation: The right side has the sign of $$b^2 - 4ac$$, since $$4a^2 > 0$$ (:ref{#real-numbers/squares-positive}). A square equals a positive number twice, $$0$$ once, a negative number never (:ref{#root-count}).

questions.question: If $$a$$ and $$c$$ have opposite signs, how many solutions does $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ have?
options: Always two, because $$-4ac > 0$$ and $$b^2 \ge 0$$, so the discriminant is positive
questions.explanation: Then $$ac < 0$$, so $$b^2 - 4ac$$ is a non-negative number plus a positive one, which is positive (:ref{#discriminant}, :ref{#root-count}).

questions.question: Without solving, what is the sum of the solutions of $$2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0$$?
questions.explanation: The sum is $$-\frac{b}{a} = \frac{5}{2}$$ and the product is $$\frac{c}{a} = -\frac{3}{2}$$ (:ref{#vieta}). Forgetting to divide by $$a$$, or the minus sign, gives the wrong answers.

questions.question: For $$x^2 + x + 1 = 0$$, what do the numbers $$-\frac{b}{a} = -1$$ and $$\frac{c}{a} = 1$$ tell you?
options: Nothing about real solutions: the discriminant is $$-3$$, so there are none to add or multiply
The solutions add to $$-1$$ and multiply to $$1$$
The equation has exactly one solution
questions.explanation: The sum and product rule assumes $$b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$$ (:ref{#vieta}). Here it is $$1 - 4 = -3 < 0$$, so there are no real solutions (:ref{#root-count}).

questions.question: What does the guide say about quadratics with a negative discriminant?
options: They have solutions among the fractions
The formula gives the wrong answer for them
They have no real solutions, but a larger number system, the complex numbers, gives them solutions
questions.explanation: No real number squares to a negative one (:ref{#real-numbers/squares-positive}), so there is no real solution (:ref{#root-count}). Just as the fractions and the real numbers filled earlier gaps, the complex numbers fill this one.

questions.question: On the graph of $$y = ax^2 + bx + c$$, where are the solutions of $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$?
questions.explanation: A point is on the $$x$$-axis exactly when $$y = 0$$, so the crossings are the $$x$$ values with $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ (:ref{#parabola}).

questions.question: What does a negative $$a$$ do to the parabola $$y = ax^2 + bx + c$$?
options: Turns it upside down, so it opens downwards and has a highest point
questions.explanation: If $$a < 0$$ the curve opens downwards and its vertex is a highest point (:ref{#parabola}).

questions.question: Writing $$ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - s)^2 + k$$ shows that the vertex is $$(s, k)$$. Why?
options: Because $$(x - s)^2$$ is never negative and is $$0$$ only at $$x = s$$
Because $$k$$ is always the largest value
Because $$s$$ is where the curve crosses the $$x$$-axis
Because the curve is a straight line near $$s$$
questions.explanation: The square is never negative (:ref{#real-numbers/squares-positive}) and is $$0$$ only at $$x = s$$, so for $$a > 0$$ the value is at least $$k$$, reached only at $$s$$ (:ref{#vertex}).

questions.question: Where is the vertex of $$y = (x + 3)^2$$?
questions.explanation: In the form $$(x - s)^2$$, here $$s = -3$$; in general $$s = -\frac{b}{2a}$$ (:ref{#vertex}). A plus sign inside the bracket moves the curve left.

questions.question: Why does a positive discriminant mean that an upward-opening parabola crosses the $$x$$-axis twice?
options: Because the vertex height is $$-\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a}$$, which is negative when $$a > 0$$, so the lowest point is below the axis
Because the vertex is then on the $$y$$-axis
questions.explanation: The vertex height $$k = c - \frac{b^2}{4a}$$ equals $$-\frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a}$$ (:ref{#vertex}). With $$a > 0$$ and a positive discriminant it is below the axis, so the U passes through the axis on the way down and again on the way up (:ref{#root-count}).

questions.question: What can a sketch of a parabola reliably tell you about its equation?
options: How many real solutions there are, and roughly where, but not their exact values
questions.explanation: A picture is a good check but a poor way of finding exact answers: $$x^2 - 2 = 0$$ crosses at $$\pm\sqrt{2}$$, which no drawing shows exactly (:ref{#parabola}).

questions.question: After putting $$u = x^2$$ in $$x^4 - 10x^2 + 9 = 0$$ and finding $$u = 1$$ or $$u = 9$$, what are the solutions?
questions.explanation: The values of $$u$$ are values of $$x^2$$, not of $$x$$. Each positive $$u$$ gives $$x = \pm\sqrt{u}$$ (:ref{#substitution-quadratic}).

questions.question: Solving $$x^4 + 3x^2 - 4 = 0$$ with $$u = x^2$$ gives $$u = -4$$ or $$u = 1$$. What does $$u = -4$$ contribute?
questions.explanation: A negative $$u$$ gives no $$x$$, because no square is negative (:ref{#substitution-quadratic}, :ref{#real-numbers/square-root-count}).

questions.question: After multiplying both sides of an equation by $$x(x + 2)$$ to clear fractions, why must you check the answers?
options: Because the step can lose solutions
Because multiplying by an expression always doubles the solutions
Because at $$x = 0$$ or $$x = -2$$ the step multiplies by $$0$$, which can let in values where a denominator is $$0$$
There is no need to check
questions.explanation: Multiplying by an expression that can be $$0$$ is not a safe step (:ref{#linear-equations/safe-steps}). It never loses solutions, but answers that make a denominator $$0$$ must be thrown out.

questions.question: Squaring both sides of $$\sqrt{2x + 3} = x$$ gives $$x = 3$$ or $$x = -1$$. Why is $$-1$$ not a solution?
options: Squaring can't tell a number from its opposite: at $$x = -1$$ the two sides are $$1$$ and $$-1$$
Because quadratics only have positive solutions
questions.explanation: Squaring keeps every solution but can add false ones (:ref{#real-numbers/squaring-sides}). A square root is never negative, so it can't equal $$-1$$; always check answers in the original equation.

questions.question: To solve $$\sqrt{x + 10} + 2 = x$$, why move the $$2$$ across before squaring?
options: Because squaring a sum is not allowed
So the root is on its own; otherwise $$(\sqrt{x + 10} + 2)^2$$ still contains a square root
Because it removes the false solutions
questions.explanation: With the root isolated, $$\sqrt{x + 10} = x - 2$$ squares to a quadratic with no roots left. It also shows $$x - 2 \ge 0$$, which rules out $$-1$$ before the check (:ref{#real-numbers/squaring-sides}).
